extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent applicants and practitioners (life sciences)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing patent claims in life sciences under the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance (IEG), using Step 1 / Step 2A / Step 2B flow and examples to decide whether claims recite statutory subject matter or judicial exceptions and whether additional limitations amount to 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are analyzed for eligibility in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation; the BRI defines embodiments to be considered in the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify one or more embodiments within the BRI (e.g., peptide+water as an embodiment of ‘peptide + pharmaceutically acceptable carrier’). Consider all embodiments when determining whether a claim or an element is a judicial exception or has markedly different characteristics; note that different embodiments may require analysis against different natural counterparts. Practice note: the BRI may encompass carriers or substitutions that change the analysis slightly, so examine alternative embodiments where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory category check
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category of invention (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is a statutory category (e.g., composition, manufacture, process, machine), proceed to determine whether it is directed to a judicial exception. Example: vaccines (compositions) and microneedle devices (manufactures) are statutory categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to any judicial exception (laws of nature, natural products, abstract ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is not directed to an exception, the claim is eligible and further Step 2A/2B evaluation is unnecessary. If it is directed to an exception, proceed to the markedly-different-characteristics (for nature-based products) analysis and then to Step 2B 'significantly more' inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature-based product analysis — select closest natural counterpart
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims reciting nature-based products, compare the claimed nature-based product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart to determine whether the claimed product has markedly different characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate natural counterpart (e.g., the virus from which a live attenuated virus was derived; for mixtures, either components or naturally occurring combinations such as soil). The chosen counterpart affects the marked-differences comparison. Guidance includes examples where the closest counterpart may be a single component or a naturally occurring combination (e.g., water/aluminum phosphate in soil).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics criterion (nature-based products)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed nature-based product must have 'markedly different characteristics' from its natural counterpart (structural, functional, or other characteristics) to avoid being a 'product of nature' exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for structural changes (e.g., mutation in nucleotide sequence) or functional/physical changes (e.g., loss of virulence, inability to replicate, changed immunogenicity, semi-solid form) that are not found in nature. Structural differences that produce functional changes are dispositive in many examples (e.g., live attenuated virus with a non-natural mutation). If no marked difference exists for at least one embodiment within the BRI, the limitation may be a 'product of nature' exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixtures and combinations — evaluate whether combination changes properties
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim recites a mixture of naturally occurring components, analyze whether combining them changes the structure, function, or other properties of the components in a marked way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the components do not occur together in nature, compare the claimed mixture to the individual components; absence of structural/functional change supports finding an exception (e.g., peptide + water where peptide retains natural structure and water retains natural properties). Conversely, an emulsion or a synergistic functional improvement (e.g., increased immunogenicity with adjuvant) can be a marked difference. Cite Funk Brothers as illustrative of mixtures that remain ineligible when each component retains the same effect it always had.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional vs. structural differences — both considered, structural often dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Both structural and functional changes are relevant to the markedly-different analysis; structural differences that yield functional changes are strong evidence of marked differences, but functional changes alone may suffice in some fact patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether functional changes (e.g., synergistic immunogenicity) are the result of, or independent from, structural changes. The guidance notes that in some cases a functional change by itself may confer eligibility, but structural change that produces the functional change is often highlighted (examples: inactivated virus chemically modified; adjuvant+peptide mixture with improved immunogenicity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A/2B procedural flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the two-step (Step 2A, Step 2B) analysis after Step 1: Step 2A asks whether the claim is directed to an exception (and applies markedly-different analysis for nature-based products); if directed to an exception, Step 2B asks whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If analysis at Step 2A shows the claim is not directed to an exception, do not perform Step 2B. If Step 2A shows the claim is directed to an exception, then proceed to Step 2B to evaluate 'significantly more' (e.g., whether recited additional elements are particular and unconventional).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — 'significantly more' (additional elements) inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying that a claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether any additional element or combination of elements ensures the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the additional elements are particular, unconventional, and provide meaningful limitations beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activity. Particular devices or unconventional combinations (e.g., a coated microneedle array used for vaccine delivery) can supply 'significantly more.' Conversely, high-level recitations or routine carriers may not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional elements must be more than mere instruction to 'apply' the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that merely instructs to apply the judicial exception using well-understood, routine, conventional activity does not make the claim 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the element confines the exception to a particular useful application (e.g., an unconventional device) or whether it just tells practitioners to use a conventional tool/procedure. Example anti-pattern: reciting 'administer and detect' with conventional techniques or generic sequencing steps at a high level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine, conventional, well-understood test (temporal and field-wide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether an element or technique was well-understood, routine, and conventional in the field at the time the invention was made and the application was filed; if so, it likely does not add 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate routine/conventional status across the field at the filing time — use by a few scientists does not make a technique routine or conventional. Example: Cool-Melt PCR used by only a few scientists was treated as not routine, so recitation of Cool-Melt PCR could be significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synergy or changed functional property as evidence of marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed combination that yields a changed or synergistic functional property (e.g., significantly increased immunogenicity) can be a marked difference from natural counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document experimental or disclosed evidence that the combination’s immunogenicity (or other functional measure) is materially different from the sum of components. Example: Peptide F + aluminum adjuvant producing 80% seroprotection vs components alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation alone does not necessarily confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely isolating a naturally occurring product does not change its structural or functional characteristics and thus does not automatically avoid the 'product of nature' exception unless isolation changes structure/function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit disclosure that isolation changed characteristics; if not, treat isolated natural products as natural products for the markedly-different analysis (e.g., isolated peptide that retains its natural structure/function remains an exception unless other changes are shown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular, unconventional devices or manufactures can supply 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of a specific, unconventional device or manufacture that is not routine in the field can confine an exception to a particular useful application and thereby contribute to eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a coated microneedle array for transcutaneous vaccine delivery was treated as an unconventional delivery device that yields 'significantly more' when combined with a peptide that is a product of nature. Evaluate whether the device was routine/conventional for the claimed use at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-focused claims may avoid product-of-nature analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim as a whole is focused on a process or method (e.g., detecting hybridization, sequencing), it may not be necessary to perform the markedly-different characteristics analysis on recited nature-based products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites process steps that are not themselves judicial exceptions (e.g., amplifying with Cool-Melt PCR and sequencing), analyze the claim as a process; if the claim as a whole is not directed to an exception, it is eligible without product analysis. Note: dependent claims that incorporate an abstract idea may still require Step 2B analysis for unconventional additional steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-level generic recitation of steps/elements generally insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting conventional steps at a high level of generality (e.g., 'sequence the amplified nucleic acids' without specific, unconventional technique limits) typically does not confer eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on broad, functional language or generic steps to supply 'significantly more.' Specificity about unconventional technique (e.g., Cool-Melt PCR) or particular parameters may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis — eligibility may be self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases, eligibility is self-evident from the claim as a whole (e.g., mechanical arrangement improving a machine) so a full Step 2A/2B analysis is unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a streamlined analysis where the claim clearly provides meaningful limitations and improvements (e.g., Fourdrinier machine arrangement using gravity to improve speed without tying up a law of nature). Document reasoning in remarks or reasons for allowance as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and contextual sensitivity of counterpart and conventionality determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations of closest natural counterpart and whether techniques/devices are routine depend on the facts and the state of the art at the time the invention was made and the application filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess contemporaneous disclosures and the state of practice across the field at filing time. Do not conflate later routine use with routine use at the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner practice guidance — record-keeping and citation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the record would benefit from clarification, examiners should add remarks to an Office action or reasons for allowance explaining the eligibility analysis and may cite analogous court decisions to support positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections should identify the exception(s) and explain why claimed nature-based products lack markedly different characteristics, and why combinations or additional elements do or do not amount to significantly more. Practice examples include citing Myriad, Funk Brothers, Mayo, Alice, and other relevant cases for analogy.
